info.title: Cloudflare D1 default database with modular provider architecture

parts.text: I'm looking to add Cloudflare D1 as default database provider so that we can have hosted database as default, and then locally hosted database only as fallback, for those users that due to privacy reason needs to have everything be privacy-first. In the future, it's likely that we provide a self-hosted model (run-it-yourself), as enterprise tier. Thus, like a principal software architect would prescribe, ensure that we put such a modular architecture in place. . Do this on a new git worktree. Finally push PR after verification.
I'll start with the brainstorming skill since this is a significant architectural change requiring design exploration.

<skill_content name="brainstorming">
# Skill: brainstorming

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

## Your First Message

Your first message is two things, in this order:

1. One line letting them know that if they'd rather skip the questions and
   have you just start, they can say so. If they take you up on it, this
   skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
   (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
   asked through the normal workflow.
2. One open question that gets them describing. Ask about a real moment
   or a concrete picture: "What's the moment you find yourself wishing
   this existed?" or "Tell me about the people who'll be in the room."

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Questions that work** anchor in specifics: "Walk me through the last
time...", "If it could only do one of these well, which?", "What would
make you wince if I got it wrong?" A guess they can correct ("I'm
guessing this is because X keeps biting you?") often beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking would help,
offer to go look: their codebase or project, their own files and data,
or the web. Say what you'd look for. They decide whether you go.

**Think wide privately.** Before you propose anything, come up with
several ideas and drop the weak ones, including any that fight what
they've told you about why. Show the comparison only when it helps them
decide.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Mark anything you're guessing as your guess; only what they said goes in
as theirs. End each chunk by asking what's wrong or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, and
they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the offer instead
(its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next message. Once
they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want, pick a size and say it in plain
words. They can override it.

| Size | The full description | Then |
|------|----------------------|------|
| A quick, clear task | the request itself | do it |
| A small change | in chat | build it through the normal workflow |
| A project with a written design | a written design document | a full plan (for software: superpowers:writing-plans) |

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

For a project, write a plain document a talented builder in the domain
could plan from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, ask. Your human partner's preferences override both.

**Builder check:** dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the full
description: in chat for a small change, the document for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After a project's document is approved, the next step is the plan. For
software, invoke superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer options to save them effort" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A description you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

1: # Agentic ODI - AI Developer Guardrails
2: 
3: This file provides system instructions and guardrails for any AI agents (or LLMs) assisting with the development of the **Agentic ODI** project. Please adhere to these guidelines to maintain consistency and align with the project's vision.
4: 
5: > **Source of Truth for ODI Methodology**: `docs/reference/Strategyn_what_is_Outcome_Driven_Innovation.pdf` by Anthony W. Ulwick (Strategyn). All ODI concepts in this project are grounded in that document. When in doubt, refer agents back to its definitions.
6: 
7: ---
8: 
9: ## 🎯 ODI Methodology Guardrails
10: 
11: This section defines how agents MUST understand and apply Outcome-Driven Innovation within this project. These are not implementation guidelines — they are domain constraints that ensure the system reflects the ODI methodology correctly.
12: 
13: ### What is Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI)?
14: 
15: ODI is a strategy and innovation process rooted in the **Jobs-to-be-Done (JTBD)** theory. Its core premise is: **people buy products and services to get a "job" done**. A "job" is the functional process a person is trying to execute — it remains stable over time, while products and technologies are point-in-time solutions that eventually become obsolete.
16: 
17: ODI achieves an **86% innovation success rate** by replacing guesswork with a rigorous, data-driven framework grounded in measurable customer needs.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ### Stage 1: Define the Market and the Job-to-be-Done
22: 
23: - A **market** is defined as: **a group of people + the functional job they are trying to get done** (e.g., "parents trying to pass on life lessons to children").
24: - A **Job-to-be-Done** is the core functional unit of analysis. It is NOT a product, solution, or feature — it is a stable human goal.
25: - **Agent rule**: Before anything else, the agent MUST help the user define the Job-to-be-Done. If no Job exists, use `add_job` to capture it. If one exists already, use `get_jobs()` to check first.
26: - ❌ **Never skip this stage**. No outcomes, steps, or scoring can be meaningful without a well-defined Job.
27: 
28: ---
29: 
30: ### Stage 2: Uncover Desired Outcomes
31: 
32: - **Desired outcomes** are the metrics customers use to measure success when getting a job done. They are the "needs" in ODI.
33: - Qualitative interviews typically uncover **50–150 desired outcome statements**.
34: - **Correct outcome statement format** (must be enforced when capturing user input):
35: 
36:   > `[Direction] + [Unit of Measure] + [Object of Control] + [Contextual Clarifier]`
37: 
38:   - ✅ **Good**: *"Minimize the time it takes to determine if the corn seeds are germinating."*
39:   - ✅ **Good**: *"Minimize the likelihood of damaging the surface when cutting."*
40:   - ❌ **Bad**: *"Make it faster"* — too vague, no direction, no measurable unit.
41:   - ❌ **Bad**: *"I want a notification"* — this is a solution/feature, not an outcome.
42: 
43: - **Agent rule**: Guide the user to express outcomes using this exact format. Reject or reframe vague statements before calling `add_outcome`. Always capture `importance` and `satisfaction` scores (1–10 scale) to enable opportunity scoring.
44: 
45: ---
46: 
47: ### Stage 3: Inventory the Job (Universal Job Map)
48: 
49: - All functional jobs decompose into **8 universal process steps** (the Universal Job Map):
50:   1. **Define** — Plan what needs to be done; select goals or resources
51:   2. **Locate** — Gather the inputs, information, or resources needed
52:   3. **Prepare** — Set up and organize everything required
53:   4. **Confirm** — Validate readiness; decide whether to proceed
54:   5. **Execute** — Perform the core task
55:   6. **Monitor** — Verify and track performance while executing
56:   7. **Modify** — Adjust or update based on feedback
57:   8. **Conclude** — Store, finish, or dispose of outputs
58: 
59: - **Agent rule**: When a user is decomposing a job into steps, reference these 8 universal stages as a guide. Steps captured via `add_step` should map to or be inspired by these universal phases. Use `get_job_map` to visualize the ordered structure.
60: - ❌ **Do not build the Job Map before capturing outcome statements** — outcomes define *what success looks like*; the job map defines *where in the process* that success matters.
61: 
62: ---
63: 
64: ### Stage 4: Discover Where the Market is Underserved (Opportunity Scoring)
65: 
66: - Each desired outcome is rated by customers on two dimensions:
67:   - **Importance** (1–10): How important is this outcome to the customer?
68:   - **Satisfaction** (1–10): How satisfied are customers with current solutions?
69: 
70: - **Opportunity Algorithm** (must be implemented correctly):
71: 
72:   ```
73:   Opportunity Score = Importance + Max(Importance - Satisfaction, 0)
74:   ```
75: 
76: - **Interpretation**:
77:   - **Score > 10**: Underserved need — significant innovation opportunity.
78:   - **Score 10**: Appropriately served — maintain, don't over-invest.
79:   - **Score < 10**: Overserved — potential for disruption via lower-cost alternatives.
80: 
81: - **Agent rule**: Always compute and surface the opportunity score when both `importance` and `satisfaction` are provided. Highlight outcomes scoring **> 10** as the highest priority innovation targets. Use `get_outcomes(job_id)` to review the full opportunity landscape.
82: 
83: ---
84: 
85: ### Stage 5: Outcome-Based Market Segmentation
86: 
87: - ODI does **not** use demographic segmentation (age, gender, region). Instead it segments the market by **which outcomes are underserved** for each group.
88: - Segments can be:
89:   - **Underserved** — high opportunity scores, want more from existing products
90:   - **Overserved** — over-investing in outcomes that aren't critical; target for disruption
91:   - **Appropriately served** — satisfied; maintain current value
92: 
93: - **Agent rule**: When the user has collected outcomes with scores, help them identify outcome clusters that represent distinct market segments. This drives targeted innovation strategy.
94: 
95: ---
96: 
97: ### Stage 6: Formulate an Innovation Strategy
98: 
99: Based on the opportunity analysis, there are three strategic paths:
100: 
101: | Strategy | When to use |
102: |---|---|
103: | **Differentiated** | Improve existing products to address high-opportunity underserved outcomes |
104: | **Disruptive** | Create low-cost solutions for overserved segments that don't need all existing features |
105: | **New-Market** | Design products for a new job that is entirely unaddressed |
106: 
107: - **Agent rule**: When the opportunity landscape is clear (outcomes scored, segments identified), guide the user to select a strategy path and align their innovation roadmap accordingly.
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: ### ⚠️ ODI Behavioral Guardrails for the Agent
112: 
113: These are absolute constraints the agent must respect:
114: 
115: | DO | DON'T |
116: |---|---|
117: | Always start by defining or confirming the Job-to-be-Done | Jump to solutions, features, or product ideas before the job is defined |
118: | Guide outcome statements with the correct format | Accept vague or solution-framed statements as valid outcomes |
119: | Compute opportunity scores when importance + satisfaction are available | Skip scoring or calculate it incorrectly |
120: | Reference the Universal Job Map when decomposing jobs | Invent arbitrary step structures disconnected from the 8 universal stages |
121: | Use outcome-based logic to identify market segments | Use demographics or assumptions to segment the market |
122: | Treat outcomes as stable, measurable success metrics | Confuse outcomes with features, preferences, or solutions |
123: | Call `get_odi_framework_guidelines` when stage guidance is needed | Guess at which stage comes next |
124: 
125: ---
126: 
127: ## 🛠 Technology Stack & Tools
128: - **Language**: Python 3.10+
129: - **MCP Framework**: `fastmcp` (Server and Client)
130: - **ASGI Server**: `uvicorn`
131: - **HTTP Client**: `httpx`
132: - **UI / Chat Client**: React + Vite (`apps/studio`), FastAPI sidecar (`apps/studio-api`)
133: - **LLM Client**: `openai` (OpenAI-compatible, used with Ollama locally)
134: - **Concurrency**: `asyncio`
135: - **Data Modeling / Validation**: `pydantic`
136: 
137: ---
138: 
139: ## 📄 README Maintenance Guardrail
140: 
141: `README.md` is the **primary human-facing entry point** for this project: a short,
142: high-level front door aimed at both users and developers. Detailed material lives
143: in `docs/` and is linked from the README. The agent MUST keep both current at all
144: times.
145: 
146: ### When to update
147: 
148: Update the relevant file whenever any of the following change:
149: 
150: | Change type | Where to update |
151: |---|---|
152: | New or removed Python file / package | `README.md` **Code Overview** |
153: | New dependency added (`pip install ...`) | `README.md` **Quick Start → Prerequisites** |
154: | New way to run the project | `README.md` **Quick Start** and `docs/living-studio.md` |
155: | New MCP tool or capability | `README.md` **Code Overview** / relevant doc |
156: | New CLI command or flag | `docs/cli.md` |
157: | New connector kind | `docs/connectors.md` |
158: | New workflow or agent instruction | `docs/living-studio.md` |
159: | Deployment URL or cloud setup changes | `docs/deployment.md` |
160: | Roadmap item completed or added | `docs/roadmap.md` |
161: | Test layout or coverage changes | `docs/development.md` |
162: 
163: ### Rules
164: 
165: - ✅ **Update docs in the same task** as the change that triggered it — never defer to a follow-up.
166: - ✅ **Keep README short**: it stays a high-level orientation page. Push detail into `docs/` and link to it rather than growing the README.
167: - ✅ **Keep the Quick Start accurate**: always reflect `uv run python scripts/dev.py` as the recommended launch command.
168: - ✅ **Keep Prerequisites up to date**: add any new `pip install` dependency immediately.
169: - ✅ **Mark Roadmap items `[x]` when completed** — do not leave stale unchecked items.
170: - ❌ **Never leave the README or `docs/` in a stale state** where documented commands or files no longer match the codebase.
171: 
172: ---
173: 
174: ## 🚧 Core Development Guardrails
175: 
176: ### 1. Model Context Protocol (MCP) Implementation
177: - **Library Choice**: ALWAYS use [`fastmcp`](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp) for building the MCP architecture. Avoid using the lower-level Anthropic `mcp` SDK directly unless there is a hyper-specific edge case that `fastmcp` does not support.
178: - **Transport Protocol**: The project is currently prototyping with **HTTP transport** (not stdio). 
179:   - The server should be initialized using `mcp.run(transport="http", ...)`.
180:   - The client must connect to the HTTP endpoint (e.g., `http://localhost:8000/mcp`).
181: - **Tool Creation**: 
182:   - Register tools on the server using the `@mcp.tool` decorator.
183:   - **CRITICAL**: Provide comprehensive docstrings and strict Python type hints for every tool parameter. Explain exactly what the tool does and what data it expects, as this metadata is fed directly to the LLM for tool discovery.
184:   - **Contract Synchronization**: Whenever you add, modify, or remove an MCP tool in `apps/mcp-server/src/agentic_odi_mcp_server/mcp_server.py`, you **MUST** simultaneously update `packages/core/src/agentic_odi_core/contract.py` (`ToolName`, `TOOL_SPECS`) and the `get_capabilities` return string. `tests/contract/test_mcp_contract.py` enforces the surface.
185: 
186: ### 2. Async / Client Practices
187: - Use `asyncio` for client execution and IO-bound tool operations.
188: - Always use the `fastmcp.Client` securely within an asynchronous context manager (`async with client:`) to ensure connections are efficiently managed and closed.
189: 
190: ### 3. Data Schema & Persistence (ODI Domain)
191: - Define all Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI) entities (e.g., *Jobs*, *Steps*, *Desired Outcomes*, *Opportunity Scores*) using `pydantic` models.
192: - When expanding the server to accept complex payloads or to query data, utilize these Pydantic models for built-in type validation and schema enforcement before the server processes the request.
193: 
194: ### 4. General Philosophy
195: - **Separation of Concerns**: Isolate the ODI data logic/retrieval from the MCP server tooling logic.
196: - **Agentic Purpose**: Remember that the tools being built are meant to be consumed by autonomous agents. Design tool interfaces that are intuitive for an LLM to call and interpret.
197: - **External connectors**: Integrations live in the `packages/connectors` workspace package. New kinds implement `agentic_odi_connectors.protocol.Connector` and register via `register_kind`. Do not write ingested records into `jobs_db` / outcomes unless a later mapping task says so.
198: - **MCP client vs ODI server**: The ODI FastMCP **server** exposes product tools. The MCP **client connector** uses `fastmcp.Client` over HTTP to ingest data from *external* MCP servers. Prefer in-memory `Client(server)` tests for that connector, same as server tests.
199: 
200: ### 5. Testing Strategy (FastMCP)
201: - **First-Class Documentation**: Treat tests as living documentation that demonstrate how features work while protecting against regressions.
202: - **Speed & Isolation**: Tests must be fast (< 1s) and self-contained. Use `@pytest.mark.integration` or `@pytest.mark.client_process` for slower, integration, or resource-dependent tests.
203: - **Structure**: This repo is a uv workspace. Mirror each project's code structure in its own `tests/` directory (e.g., `apps/mcp-server/src/agentic_odi_mcp_server/mcp_server.py` -> `apps/mcp-server/tests/test_server_tools.py`, `packages/connectors/src/agentic_odi_connectors/mcp/connector.py` -> `packages/connectors/tests/test_mcp_connector.py`).
204: - **Atomic Tests**: Each test must verify exactly one specific behavior with clear intent in test names and assertions. Avoid multi-behavior tests.
205: - **In-Memory Testing (Preferred)**: Favor testing functionality deterministically by passing the `FastMCP` server directly into the `Client(server)` instance. This runs in-memory without network overhead for deterministic and lightning-fast execution.
206: - **Transport Testing (When Needed)**: For HTTP/SSE network transport tests, prefer the isolated in-process `fastmcp.utilities.tests.run_server_async(server)` context manager over subprocess testing (which uses `run_server_in_process` and is slower to debug).
207: - **Data Assertions**: Utilize `inline-snapshot` (`snapshot()`) for assessing complex data structures like tool API JSON schemas or expected responses.

(End of file - total 207 lines)
</content>

  5. **Execute** — Perform the core task
  6. **Monitor** — Verify and track performance while executing
  7. **Modify** — Adjust or update based on feedback
  8. **Conclude** — Store, finish, or dispose of outputs

- **Agent rule**: When a user is decomposing a job into steps, reference these 8 universal stages as a guide. Steps captured via `add_step` should map to or be inspired by these universal phases. Use `get_job_map` to visualize the ordered structure.
- ❌ **Do not build the Job Map before capturing outcome statements** — outcomes define *what success looks like*; the job map defines *where in the process* that success matters.

---

### Stage 4: Discover Where the Market is Underserved (Opportunity Scoring)

- Each desired outcome is rated by customers on two dimensions:
  - **Importance** (1–10): How important is this outcome to the customer?
  - **Satisfaction** (1–10): How satisfied are customers with current solutions?

- **Opportunity Algorithm** (must be implemented correctly):

  ```
  Opportunity Score = Importance + Max(Importance - Satisfaction, 0)
  ```

- **Interpretation**:
  - **Score > 10**: Underserved need — significant innovation opportunity.
  - **Score 10**: Appropriately served — maintain, don't over-invest.
  - **Score < 10**: Overserved — potential for disruption via lower-cost alternatives.

- **Agent rule**: Always compute and surface the opportunity score when both `importance` and `satisfaction` are provided. Highlight outcomes scoring **> 10** as the highest priority innovation targets. Use `get_outcomes(job_id)` to review the full opportunity landscape.

---

### Stage 5: Outcome-Based Market Segmentation

- ODI does **not** use demographic segmentation (age, gender, region). Instead it segments the market by **which outcomes are underserved** for each group.
- Segments can be:
  - **Underserved** — high opportunity scores, want more from existing products
  - **Overserved** — over-investing in outcomes that aren't critical; target for disruption
  - **Appropriately served** — satisfied; maintain current value

- **Agent rule**: When the user has collected outcomes with scores, help them identify outcome clusters that represent distinct market segments. This drives targeted innovation strategy.

---

### Stage 6: Formulate an Innovation Strategy

Based on the opportunity analysis, there are three strategic paths:

| Strategy | When to use |
|---|---|
| **Differentiated** | Improve existing products to address high-opportunity underserved outcomes |
| **Disruptive** | Create low-cost solutions for overserved segments that don't need all existing features |
| **New-Market** | Design products for a new job that is entirely unaddressed |

- **Agent rule**: When the opportunity landscape is clear (outcomes scored, segments identified), guide the user to select a strategy path and align their innovation roadmap accordingly.

---

### ⚠️ ODI Behavioral Guardrails for the Agent

These are absolute constraints the agent must respect:

| DO | DON'T |
|---|---|
| Always start by defining or confirming the Job-to-be-Done | Jump to solutions, features, or product ideas before the job is defined |
| Guide outcome statements with the correct format | Accept vague or solution-framed statements as valid outcomes |
| Compute opportunity scores when importance + satisfaction are available | Skip scoring or calculate it incorrectly |
| Reference the Universal Job Map when decomposing jobs | Invent arbitrary step structures disconnected from the 8 universal stages |
| Use outcome-based logic to identify market segments | Use demographics or assumptions to segment the market |
| Treat outcomes as stable, measurable success metrics | Confuse outcomes with features, preferences, or solutions |
| Call `get_odi_framework_guidelines` when stage guidance is needed | Guess at which stage comes next |

---

## 🛠 Technology Stack & Tools
- **Language**: Python 3.10+
- **MCP Framework**: `fastmcp` (Server and Client)
- **ASGI Server**: `uvicorn`
- **HTTP Client**: `httpx`
- **UI / Chat Client**: React + Vite (`apps/studio`), FastAPI sidecar (`apps/studio-api`)
- **LLM Client**: `openai` (OpenAI-compatible, used with Ollama locally)
- **Concurrency**: `asyncio`
- **Data Modeling / Validation**: `pydantic`

---

## 📄 README Maintenance Guardrail

`README.md` is the **primary human-facing entry point** for this project: a short,
high-level front door aimed at both users and developers. Detailed material lives
in `docs/` and is linked from the README. The agent MUST keep both current at all
times.

### When to update

Update the relevant file whenever any of the following change:

| Change type | Where to update |
|---|---|
| New or removed Python file / package | `README.md` **Code Overview** |
| New dependency added (`pip install ...`) | `README.md` **Quick Start → Prerequisites** |
| New way to run the project | `README.md` **Quick Start** and `docs/living-studio.md` |
| New MCP tool or capability | `README.md` **Code Overview** / relevant doc |
| New CLI command or flag | `docs/cli.md` |
| New connector kind | `docs/connectors.md` |
| New workflow or agent instruction | `docs/living-studio.md` |
| Deployment URL or cloud setup changes | `docs/deployment.md` |
| Roadmap item completed or added | `docs/roadmap.md` |
| Test layout or coverage changes | `docs/development.md` |

### Rules

- ✅ **Update docs in the same task** as the change that triggered it — never defer to a follow-up.
- ✅ **Keep README short**: it stays a high-level orientation page. Push detail into `docs/` and link to it rather than growing the README.
- ✅ **Keep the Quick Start accurate**: always reflect `uv run python scripts/dev.py` as the recommended launch command.
- ✅ **Keep Prerequisites up to date**: add any new `pip install` dependency immediately.
- ✅ **Mark Roadmap items `[x]` when completed** — do not leave stale unchecked items.
- ❌ **Never leave the README or `docs/` in a stale state** where documented commands or files no longer match the codebase.

---

## 🚧 Core Development Guardrails

### 1. Model Context Protocol (MCP) Implementation
- **Library Choice**: ALWAYS use [`fastmcp`](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp) for building the MCP architecture. Avoid using the lower-level Anthropic `mcp` SDK directly unless there is a hyper-specific edge case that `fastmcp` does not support.
- **Transport Protocol**: The project is currently prototyping with **HTTP transport** (not stdio). 
  - The server should be initialized using `mcp.run(transport="http", ...)`.
  - The client must connect to the HTTP endpoint (e.g., `http://localhost:8000/mcp`).
- **Tool Creation**: 
  - Register tools on the server using the `@mcp.tool` decorator.
  - **CRITICAL**: Provide comprehensive docstrings and strict Python type hints for every tool parameter. Explain exactly what the tool does and what data it expects, as this metadata is fed directly to the LLM for tool discovery.
  - **Contract Synchronization**: Whenever you add, modify, or remove an MCP tool in `apps/mcp-server/src/agentic_odi_mcp_server/mcp_server.py`, you **MUST** simultaneously update `packages/core/src/agentic_odi_core/contract.py` (`ToolName`, `TOOL_SPECS`) and the `get_capabilities` return string. `tests/contract/test_mcp_contract.py` enforces the surface.

### 2. Async / Client Practices
- Use `asyncio` for client execution and IO-bound tool operations.
- Always use the `fastmcp.Client` securely within an asynchronous context manager (`async with client:`) to ensure connections are efficiently managed and closed.

### 3. Data Schema & Persistence (ODI Domain)
- Define all Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI) entities (e.g., *Jobs*, *Steps*, *Desired Outcomes*, *Opportunity Scores*) using `pydantic` models.
- When expanding the server to accept complex payloads or to query data, utilize these Pydantic models for built-in type validation and schema enforcement before the server processes the request.

### 4. General Philosophy
- **Separation of Concerns**: Isolate the ODI data logic/retrieval from the MCP server tooling logic.
- **Agentic Purpose**: Remember that the tools being built are meant to be consumed by autonomous agents. Design tool interfaces that are intuitive for an LLM to call and interpret.
- **External connectors**: Integrations live in the `packages/connectors` workspace package. New kinds implement `agentic_odi_connectors.protocol.Connector` and register via `register_kind`. Do not write ingested records into `jobs_db` / outcomes unless a later mapping task says so.
- **MCP client vs ODI server**: The ODI FastMCP **server** exposes product tools. The MCP **client connector** uses `fastmcp.Client` over HTTP to ingest data from *external* MCP servers. Prefer in-memory `Client(server)` tests for that connector, same as server tests.

### 5. Testing Strategy (FastMCP)
- **First-Class Documentation**: Treat tests as living documentation that demonstrate how features work while protecting against regressions.
- **Speed & Isolation**: Tests must be fast (< 1s) and self-contained. Use `@pytest.mark.integration` or `@pytest.mark.client_process` for slower, integration, or resource-dependent tests.
- **Structure**: This repo is a uv workspace. Mirror each project's code structure in its own `tests/` directory (e.g., `apps/mcp-server/src/agentic_odi_mcp_server/mcp_server.py` -> `apps/mcp-server/tests/test_server_tools.py`, `packages/connectors/src/agentic_odi_connectors/mcp/connector.py` -> `packages/connectors/tests/test_mcp_connector.py`).
- **Atomic Tests**: Each test must verify exactly one specific behavior with clear intent in test names and assertions. Avoid multi-behavior tests.
- **In-Memory Testing (Preferred)**: Favor testing functionality deterministically by passing the `FastMCP` server directly into the `Client(server)` instance. This runs in-memory without network overhead for deterministic and lightning-fast execution.
- **Transport Testing (When Needed)**: For HTTP/SSE network transport tests, prefer the isolated in-process `fastmcp.utilities.tests.run_server_async(server)` context manager over subprocess testing (which uses `run_server_in_process` and is slower to debug).
- **Data Assertions**: Utilize `inline-snapshot` (`snapshot()`) for assessing complex data structures like tool API JSON schemas or expected responses.

[project]
name = "agentic-odi"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI): an MCP server, chat client, CLI, and external connectors."
requires-python = ">=3.10"

[tool.uv]
package = false

[tool.uv.workspace]
members = [
    "apps/cli",
    "apps/mcp-server",
    "apps/studio-api",
    "packages/connectors",
    "packages/core",
]

[dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "bandit==1.9.4",
    "mypy==2.4.0",
    "pyinstaller==6.22.3",
    "pytest==9.1.1",
    "pytest-asyncio==1.4.0",
    "pytest-cov==7.1.0",
    "ruff==0.17.0",
    "pillow==12.3.0",
]

[tool.bandit]
exclude_dirs = [".venv", "tests", ".worktrees", "node_modules"]

[tool.ruff]
line-length = 100
target-version = "py310"
# Vendored Superpowers skills are third-party content. Their Markdown code
# fences are examples, not project Python, so Ruff must not lint or reformat
# them (and `npx skills update` would overwrite any local edits anyway).
extend-exclude = [".agents/skills", ".worktrees"]

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = ["E4", "E7", "E9", "F", "I", "UP", "B", "BLE"]

[tool.mypy]
python_version = "3.10"
ignore_missing_imports = true
plugins = ["pydantic.mypy"]
disable_error_code = ["prop-decorator"]

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
asyncio_mode = "strict"
pythonpath = ["."]
testpaths = ["apps", "packages", "tests", "website"]

[tool.coverage.run]
source = [
    "agentic_odi_cli",
    "agentic_odi_connectors",
    "agentic_odi_core",
    "agentic_odi_mcp_server",
    "agentic_odi_studio_api",
]

display.text:
# Repository Architecture

Agentic ODI is a uv workspace with a single root `pyproject.toml` for shared tooling. Python distributions are imported by their stable `agentic_odi_*` package names; directory layout does not leak into imports.

## Layout

```text
apps/
  cli/            agentic_odi_cli         Typer CLI: local SQLite or remote MCP
  mcp-server/     agentic_odi_mcp_server  FastMCP server over HTTP
  studio-api/     agentic_odi_studio_api  FastAPI sidecar for the Studio SPA
  studio/         React + TypeScript + Vite SPA and Tauri 2 shell
packages/
  core/           agentic_odi_core        Domain, services, repositories, contract
  connectors/     agentic_odi_connectors  MCP client connectors and catalog
infra/cloudflare/ Worker + Wrangler config for the free-plan deployment
scripts/          Dev launcher, binary build, installer checks
tests/            Cross-package contract and launcher tests only
docs/             Architecture, reference material, Superpowers artifacts
packaging/        PyInstaller spec for the CLI binary
```

## Dependency Direction

```text
apps/cli ──────────────┐
apps/mcp-server ───────┼──▶ packages/core
apps/studio-api ───────┘         ▲
                                 │
apps/cli ──────────────▶ packages/connectors
```

- `packages/core` depends on no other workspace package.
- `packages/connectors` depends on `core` only where it needs shared models.
- Every runnable app may depend on `core`; none of them imports another app.
- The React SPA only talks to `apps/studio-api` over `/api`; it never calls MCP or the LLM directly.

## Persistence

- `SQLiteRepository` is the production default for the CLI, MCP server, and Studio API.
- The default database is `~/.agentic-odi/odi.db`, overridable with `AGENTIC_ODI_DB`.
- `build_repository()` chooses SQLite by default and `InMemoryRepository` when `AGENTIC_ODI_DB=:memory:`, which is what tests use.
- The CLI selects its backend with `--backend local|mcp` or `AGENTIC_ODI_BACKEND`.
- The Studio API selects `local` (direct service calls) or `mcp` (passthrough) with `AGENTIC_ODI_BACKEND` or `create_app(backend=...)`.

## MCP Contract

`packages/core/src/agentic_odi_core/contract.py` owns `ToolName`, `ToolSpec`, `TOOL_SPECS`, and `TOOL_NAMES`. The live FastMCP registry is asserted against it by `tests/contract/test_mcp_contract.py`; the CLI's local handlers are checked by `tests/contract/test_cli_contract.py`.

## Entry Points

| Command | Module |
|---|---|
| `agentic-odi` | `agentic_odi_cli.cli:app` |
| `agentic-odi-server` / `agentic-odi-mcp-server` | `agentic_odi_mcp_server.mcp_server:main` |
| `agentic-odi-studio-api` | `agentic_odi_studio_api.main:main` |
| `uv run python scripts/dev.py` | Dev launcher (MCP + Studio API) |

## Related

- [Data flow](data-flow.md)
- [Testing](testing.md)

<content>
1: # Data Flow
2: 
3: ## Sources of Truth
4: 
5: | Layer | Owns | Persists |
6: |---|---|---|
7: | `packages/core` | `Job`, `Step`, `Outcome`, `CustomerOutcome`, `ODIService`, repository protocol | SQLite event log + snapshots |
8: | `apps/mcp-server` | MCP tool adapters over `ODIService` | `build_repository()` selects SQLite in production and in-memory for `AGENTIC_ODI_DB=:memory:` |
9: | `apps/studio-api` | Studio API, canvas projection, chat tool loop | Via the same repository when the local backend is active |
10: | `apps/studio` | Presentation state, optimistic canvas updates | Browser cache only |
11: | `apps/cli` | Terminal rendering, local/remote backend selection | SQLite directly for `local`, no local writes for `mcp` |
12: 
13: ## Write Paths
14: 
15: ### Local CLI
16: 
17: ```text
18: agentic-odi customer-outcomes add
19:   -> LocalBackend
20:   -> ODIService
21:   -> SQLiteRepository
22:   -> IntentStore (append) + snapshot refresh
23: ```
24: 
25: ### MCP
26: 
27: ```text
28: MCP client / Studio MCP mode / CLI --backend mcp
29:   -> FastMCP tool
30:   -> ODIService
31:   -> configured Repository
32: ```
33: 
34: `apps/mcp-server` builds its repository once at import time with `build_repository()`. Production uses SQLite; tests set `AGENTIC_ODI_DB=:memory:` (the root test suite does this in `tests/conftest.py`).
35: 
36: ### Studio API
37: 
38: ```text
39: apps/studio SPA
40:   -> /api/canvas, /api/steps, /api/outcomes
41:   -> backend=local: ODIService -> Repository
42:   -> backend=mcp:   call_mcp_tool -> MCP server -> ODIService -> Repository
43: 
44: apps/studio SPA
45:   -> /api/chat
46:   -> stream_chat -> OpenAI-compatible LLM -> MCP tool calls
47: ```
48: 
49: The SPA sends `mcp_url` with every data request for compatibility. In `local` mode the sidecar ignores it; in `mcp` mode it is required for canvas and mutations.
50: 
51: ## Read Paths
52: 
53: ```text
54: ODIService.get_jobs / get_job_map / get_outcomes
55:   -> Repository read-through state

# Data Flow

## Sources of Truth

| Layer | Owns | Persists |
|---|---|---|
| `packages/core` | `Job`, `Step`, `Outcome`, `CustomerOutcome`, `ODIService`, repository protocol | SQLite event log + snapshots |
| `apps/mcp-server` | MCP tool adapters over `ODIService` | `build_repository()` selects SQLite in production and in-memory for `AGENTIC_ODI_DB=:memory:` |
| `apps/studio-api` | Studio API, canvas projection, chat tool loop | Via the same repository when the local backend is active |
| `apps/studio` | Presentation state, optimistic canvas updates | Browser cache only |
| `apps/cli` | Terminal rendering, local/remote backend selection | SQLite directly for `local`, no local writes for `mcp` |

## Write Paths

### Local CLI

```text
agentic-odi customer-outcomes add
  -> LocalBackend
  -> ODIService
  -> SQLiteRepository
  -> IntentStore (append) + snapshot refresh
```

### MCP

```text
MCP client / Studio MCP mode / CLI --backend mcp
  -> FastMCP tool
  -> ODIService
  -> configured Repository
```

`apps/mcp-server` builds its repository once at import time with `build_repository()`. Production uses SQLite; tests set `AGENTIC_ODI_DB=:memory:` (the root test suite does this in `tests/conftest.py`).

### Studio API

```text
apps/studio SPA
  -> /api/canvas, /api/steps, /api/outcomes
  -> backend=local: ODIService -> Repository
  -> backend=mcp:   call_mcp_tool -> MCP server -> ODIService -> Repository

apps/studio SPA
  -> /api/chat
  -> stream_chat -> OpenAI-compatible LLM -> MCP tool calls
```

The SPA sends `mcp_url` with every data request for compatibility. In `local` mode the sidecar ignores it; in `mcp` mode it is required for canvas and mutations.

## Read Paths

```text
ODIService.get_jobs / get_job_map / get_outcomes
  -> Repository read-through state
  -> Pydantic models
  -> JSON (CLI --json, MCP text payload, Studio canvas)
```

The Studio canvas falls back to the demo seed only in `mcp` mode when MCP is unreachable or returns no jobs. `local` mode returns exactly what is in the local database, including an empty canvas.

## Configuration

| Variable | Used by | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `AGENTIC_ODI_DB` | core SQLite repository | `~/.agentic-odi/odi.db` |
| `AGENTIC_ODI_BACKEND` | CLI, Studio API | `local` |
| `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL` | CLI, Studio defaults | `http://localhost:8000/mcp` |
| `AGENTIC_ODI_STUDIO_DIST` | Studio API, dev launcher | `apps/studio/dist` |
| `AGENTIC_ODI_REPO_ROOT` | Tauri shell | auto-detected |
| `AGENTIC_ODI_BASE_URL` | CLI chat, Studio chat | `http://localhost:8001/v1` |
| `AGENTIC_ODI_MODEL` | CLI chat, Studio chat | `local-tools-model` |
| `AGENTIC_ODI_API_KEY` | CLI chat, Studio chat | `local` |

## Trust Boundaries

- The SPA runs in a browser or Tauri webview and only trusts the sidecar origin.
- The sidecar may reach MCP and the LLM; CORS is restricted to known Studio origins.
- MCP is an HTTP service with no authentication in local development. Do not expose it directly to the internet; the Cloudflare setup tunnels the sidecar, not MCP.

"""Append-only Intent Store (CTO specification)."""

import json
import sqlite3
from datetime import datetime


class IntentStore:
    def __init__(self, db_path: str = "intent_store.db", check_same_thread: bool = True) -> None:
        # Connect to SQLite in WAL mode for high-performance concurrency
        self.conn = sqlite3.connect(db_path, check_same_thread=check_same_thread)
        self.conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;")
        self._init_db()

    def _init_db(self) -> None:
        """Creates an immutable, append-only event table."""
        with self.conn:
            self.conn.execute(
                """
                CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS events (
                    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
                    timestamp TEXT NOT NULL,
                    event_type TEXT NOT NULL,
                    payload TEXT NOT NULL
                )
            """
            )

    def append(self, event_type: str, payload: dict) -> None:
        """Appends a new event to the stream (Immutable write)."""
        timestamp = datetime.utcnow().isoformat()
        payload_json = json.dumps(payload)
        with self.conn:
            self.conn.execute(
                "INSERT INTO events (timestamp, event_type, payload) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
                (timestamp, event_type, payload_json),
            )

    def get_stream(self) -> list[dict]:
        """Retrieves the full chronological event stream for AI reasoning."""
        cursor = self.conn.cursor()
        cursor.execute("SELECT id, timestamp, event_type, payload FROM events ORDER BY id ASC")
        return [
            {
                "id": row[0],
                "timestamp": row[1],
                "type": row[2],
                "payload": json.loads(row[3]) if row[3] else {},
            }
            for row in cursor.fetchall()
        ]

    def clear(self) -> None:
        """Clear all events (for testing)."""
        with self.conn:
            self.conn.execute("DELETE FROM events")

    def close(self) -> None:
        self.conn.close()

sidecar's CORS list is not involved.

```bash
# 1. Build the SPA that the Worker uploads as static assets
npm --prefix apps/studio ci
npm --prefix apps/studio run build

# 2. Terminal A — MCP server (:8000) + sidecar (:8100)
python scripts/dev.py

# 3. Terminal B — free public URL for the sidecar (no account required)
cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:8100
# copy the https://<random>.trycloudflare.com URL it prints

# 4. Store the URL on the Worker, then deploy
npx wrangler secret put SIDECAR_URL   # paste the trycloudflare URL
npx wrangler deploy
```

Workers Builds settings (Workers & Pages → your Worker → Settings → Builds):

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Root directory | `/` |
| Build command | `npm --prefix apps/studio ci && npm --prefix apps/studio run build` |
| Deploy command | `npx wrangler deploy` |

A Worker has no run command: the Worker script runs on Cloudflare. Set `name` in
`wrangler.jsonc` to the Worker you created before the first deploy.

> [!NOTE]
> The sidecar runs on your machine, so the Worker only works while
> `python scripts/dev.py` and the Quick Tunnel are running. Quick Tunnel URLs
> change on every restart — update the secret with
> `npx wrangler secret put SIDECAR_URL`. Chat also needs a reachable
> OpenAI-compatible endpoint in the Studio's **Settings**; the canvas, job map,
> and impact simulation work without one.

# Agentic ODI [![CI](https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/alehar9320/agentic-odi/branch/main/graph/badge.svg)](https://codecov.io/gh/alehar9320/agentic-odi) [![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.10%2B-blue.svg)](https://www.python.org/downloads/) [![uv](https://img.shields.io/badge/uv-managed-green)](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) [![Ruff](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/astral-sh/ruff/main/assets/badge/v2.json)](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff) [![FastMCP](https://img.shields.io/badge/FastMCP-powered-orange)](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp) [![pytest](https://img.shields.io/badge/tests-pytest-blue)](https://pytest.org) [![MCP](https://img.shields.io/badge/Model%20Context%20Protocol-enabled-8A2BE2)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) > **[![Experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/Experimental-1e293b?style=for-the-badge)](https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi)** > **Experimental test to learn and evaluate the feasibility of utilizing Model Context Protocol (MCP) for Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI) specifications.**
--- **Agentic ODI** explores how the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) can turn [Outcome-Driven Innovation](https://strategyn.com/outcome-driven-innovation/) into a live, agent-queryable source of context. Instead of feeding LLMs disconnected prompts, an MCP-powered ODI server acts as the "brain" of customer needs — letting agents invent, evaluate, and ideate solutions anchored in verified, measurable customer outcomes (Job Maps, Desired Outcomes, and Opportunity Scores). This repository is an experimental testbed for understanding server–client MCP communication streams, built on [`FastMCP`](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp). We don't publish dates. This page changes when the code does. ## Code Overview A [uv workspace](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/workspaces/) with shared tooling at the root. Packages live in `packages/`, runnable services in `apps/`, and deployment assets in `infra/`: | Path | Distribution | Description | |---|---|---| | **`packages/core/`** | `agentic-odi-core` | Domain models, the `ODIService` business-logic layer, repository implementations (in-memory and SQLite), the shared MCP tool contract, and ODI opportunity-score computation. | | **`packages/connectors/`** | `agentic-odi-connectors` | Pluggable MCP and REST connectors with presets and an ingest sink. | | **`apps/mcp-server/`** | `agentic-odi-mcp-server` | FastMCP server exposing Jobs, Steps, Desired Outcomes, Customer Outcomes, Evidence, and context tools over HTTP. Persists to SQLite by default. | | **`apps/studio-api/`** | `agentic-odi-studio-api` | FastAPI **Living Studio sidecar**. Serves config, health, canvas data, local mutations, MCP passthrough, SSE chat, and the built SPA. | | **`apps/cli/`** | `agentic-odi-cli` | Typer CLI with interactive chat plus full entity CRUD, `schema`, `connectors`, and local-first (`--backend local`) or remote (`--backend mcp`) data access. | | **`apps/studio/`** | React + TypeScript + Vite | **The Living Studio** SPA and Tauri 2 desktop shell. | | **`infra/cloudflare/`** | Worker | Free-plan Workers Static Assets deployment and sidecar tunnel. | | **`scripts/`** | — | Dev launcher, binary build, installer tests. | | **`tests/contract/`** | — | Cross-package MCP contract tests. | See [Architecture](docs/architecture/README.md) for the dependency graph, data flow, and testing strategy. ## Quick Start **Prerequisites:** Python 3.10+ and the [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) package manager. ```bash # Install the entire workspace (all five Python projects plus dev tooling) uv sync --all-packages # Build the Studio SPA, then launch the MCP server and Living Studio together npm --prefix apps/studio run build python scripts/dev.py ``` | Service | URL | |---|---| | MCP Server | http://localhost:8000/mcp | | The Living Studio | http://127.0.0.1:8100 | For hot reload, `npm --prefix apps/studio run dev:full` starts the MCP server, the sidecar, and Vite together on http://localhost:5173. For the desktop app, use `npm --prefix apps/studio run tauri dev`. See [Running The Living Studio](docs/living-studio.md). The Studio opens as a conversation: describe a job or a customer frustration, or use the left drawer to open the opportunity landscape, job map, impact simulation, evidence, and capture panels beside the chat. The Studio needs an OpenAI-compatible LLM with tool-calling support to drive its agent — see the [Local LLM Backend](docs/local-llm.md). ### CLI at a glance The CLI is local-first, so data commands work without a running server: ```bash python -m agentic_odi_cli --version # print the Agentic ODI version python -m agentic_odi_cli --help # show available options and commands python -m agentic_odi_cli # start interactive chat in a terminal agentic-odi jobs list # Jobs-to-be-Done agentic-odi steps list --job-id agentic-odi desired-outcomes list --job-id agentic-odi customer-outcomes list agentic-odi evidence list --job-id agentic-odi schema # canonical JSON schema for every entity agentic-odi score 8 2 # ODI opportunity score → 14.00 ``` Add `--backend mcp` to route data commands through a running MCP server (`python -m agentic_odi_mcp_server`). See the [CLI Reference](docs/cli.md). ### Install the binary Prebuilt binaries are available for Linux, macOS, and Windows: ```bash curl -fsSL https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh ``` The installer symlinks `odi`, `odipm`, `odi-cli`, and `agentic-odi` into `~/.local/bin/`. See [Installation](docs/installation.md) for the install layout, updates, and release automation. ## Documentation | Guide | Contents | |---|---| | [CLI Reference](docs/cli.md) | Backends, interactive chat, Jobs/Steps/desired Outcomes/Customer Outcomes/evidence, `connectors`, scoring, environment variables | | [External Connectors](docs/connectors.md) | The MCP ingest connector, presets, and the `Connector` protocol | | [Running The Living Studio](docs/living-studio.md) | Run modes, desktop signing and updates, agent-driven testing (`/dev`, `/test`) | | [Local LLM Backend](docs/local-llm.md) | Running a local OpenAI-compatible model with tool calling | | [Development](docs/development.md) | Lint, format, type checks, frontend checks, tests and the coverage map | | [Architecture](docs/architecture/README.md) | Workspace layout, dependency direction, data flow, and testing | | [Installation](docs/installation.md) | Binary install, updater behavior, and release automation | | [Deployment](docs/deployment.md) | Hosted chat UI, the MCP server endpoint, and the free-plan Cloudflare Worker | | [Roadmap](docs/roadmap.md) | Completed and upcoming milestones | | [Superpowers](docs/superpowers.md) | Pi, OpenCode, and Freebuff integration | ## Contributing Contributions are welcome! This project uses [Ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/) for linting and formatting and [pytest](https://pytest.org/) for tests. Make sure your change passes the [lint, format, and test checks](docs/development.md) before opening a pull request. ## License No license has been specified for this repository yet. Until one is added, all rights reserved by the maintainers. Please reach out before reuse or redistribution. ---
*Let's build AI that builds what people actually need.*

Local-first CRDT-ish log. This enables offline, team, cross-device, privacy. This is the principal-architect choice: sync at the event log layer, not ORM row layer. This is clean and future-proof for self-hosted.

Updates are events not row mutations, so last-write-wins by server order; per-field updates. Deletion events. Ordering: server total order after push. Dedupe with event UUID. """MCP hydration and passthrough writes, ported from the Streamlit app."""

from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import contextlib
import json
from typing import Any

from agentic_odi_core import ODIService, ToolName
from fastapi import HTTPException
from fastmcp import Client as McpClient

from agentic_odi_studio_api.studio.probes import is_endpoint_reachable
from agentic_odi_studio_api.studio.seed import seed_payload

MCP_CALL_TIMEOUT = 3.0


async def fetch_canvas(mcp_url: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Fetch live canvas data from FastMCP, falling back to the seed prototype."""
    jobs: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    outcomes: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    steps: list[dict[str, Any]] = []

    if not is_endpoint_reachable(mcp_url, timeout=0.3):
        return {**seed_payload(), "source": "seed"}

    with contextlib.suppress(Exception):
        mcp_client = McpClient(mcp_url)
        async with mcp_client:
            raw_jobs = await asyncio.wait_for(
                mcp_client.call_tool(ToolName.GET_JOBS.value, {}), timeout=1.5
            )
            try:
                parsed_jobs = json.loads(str(raw_jobs))
                if isinstance(parsed_jobs, list):
                    jobs = parsed_jobs
            except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001
                jobs = []

            for job in jobs:
                job_id = job.get("id")
                if not job_id:
                    continue

                with contextlib.suppress(Exception):
                    raw_steps = await asyncio.wait_for(
                        mcp_client.call_tool(ToolName.GET_JOB_MAP.value, {"job_id": job_id}),
                        timeout=1.0,
                    )
                    parsed_steps = json.loads(str(raw_steps))
                    if isinstance(parsed_steps, list):
                        steps.extend(parsed_steps)

                with contextlib.suppress(Exception):
                    raw_outcomes = await asyncio.wait_for(
                        mcp_client.call_tool(ToolName.GET_OUTCOMES.value, {"job_id": job_id}),
                        timeout=1.0,
                    )
                    parsed_outcomes = json.loads(str(raw_outcomes))
                    if isinstance(parsed_outcomes, list):
                        outcomes.extend(parsed_outcomes)

    if not jobs:
        return {**seed_payload(), "source": "seed"}

    return {"jobs": jobs, "steps": steps, "outcomes": outcomes, "source": "mcp"}


def fetch_local_canvas(service: ODIService) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Read the canvas directly from the local service, no HTTP round trip."""
    jobs = [job.model_dump() for job in service.get_jobs()]
    steps: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    outcomes: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    for job in jobs:
        job_id = job["id"]
        steps.extend(step.model_dump() for step in service.get_job_map(job_id))
        outcomes.extend(outcome.model_dump() for outcome in service.get_outcomes(job_id))
    return {"jobs": jobs, "steps": steps, "outcomes": outcomes, "source": "local"}


async def call_mcp_tool(mcp_url: str, tool: str, arguments: dict[str, Any]) -> str:
    """Invoke an MCP tool, surfacing failures as HTTP 502."""
    if not is_endpoint_reachable(mcp_url, timeout=0.3):
        raise HTTPException(status_code=502, detail=f"MCP server unreachable at {mcp_url}")

    try:
        async with McpClient(mcp_url) as mcp_client:
            result = await asyncio.wait_for(
                mcp_client.call_tool(tool, arguments), timeout=MCP_CALL_TIMEOUT
            )
            return str(result)
    except HTTPException:
        raise
    except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
        raise HTTPException(status_code=502, detail=f"Error calling {tool}: {exc}") from exc

1: # Running The Living Studio
2: 
3: **The Living Studio** is the conversational GUI for Outcome-Driven Innovation:
4: an interactive Opportunity Landscape, Universal Job Map, WYSIWYG Impact
5: Simulation, and Causal Lineage inspection, paired with an autonomous agent
6: connected to the MCP server.
7: 
8: The Studio runs three ways. All of them serve the same SPA, which talks only to
9: the sidecar on `http://127.0.0.1:8100` — the SPA never contacts MCP or the LLM
10: directly.
11: 
12: ## Architecture
13: 
14: ```text
15: ┌────────────────────────────┐  /api (JSON)  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
16: │  Living Studio SPA         │ ────────────▶ │  apps/studio-api (sidecar)    │
17: │  React + TS + Vite         │  /api/chat    │  FastAPI on 127.0.0.1:8100    │
18: │  (browser or Tauri webview)│ ◀──────────── │  - config / health / canvas   │
19: └────────────────────────────┘  SSE stream   │  - steps / outcomes (via MCP) │
20:                                              │  - /api/chat (LLM tool-loop)  │
21:                                              └───────────────┬───────────────┘
22:                                                              │ MCP (HTTP)
23:                                                              ▼
24:                                              ┌───────────────────────────────┐
25:                                              │  apps/mcp-server :8000/mcp    │
26:                                              └───────────────────────────────┘
27:                                                              ▲
28:                                                              │ OpenAI-compatible
29:                                              ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
30:                                              │  Your local LLM backend       │
31:                                              └───────────────────────────────┘
32: ```
33: 
34: ## Interface
35: 
36: The Studio opens as a conversation, not a dashboard.
37: 
38: | Surface | What it does |
39: |---|---|
40: | **Hero** | One rotating headline above the composer: a greeting (time of day, plus your name if you set one in Settings), what is already on the canvas, or what the studio can do. It cycles every few seconds and stays still under `prefers-reduced-motion`. |
41: | **Suggestion pills** | Below the headline. Some open a workspace panel (landscape, simulate, capture), others start a conversation. They change as the canvas fills up. |
42: | **Composer** | Docked at the bottom of the transcript. `Enter` sends, `Shift`+`Enter` adds a line, `Cmd/Ctrl`+`K` focuses it, and the send button becomes a stop button while a reply streams. |
43: | **Drawer** (left) | New conversation, the five workspace panels, live model/MCP status, and Settings. Collapses to an icon rail with `Cmd/Ctrl`+`B`; becomes an overlay sheet on narrow screens. |
44: | **Workspace panel** (right) | The classic UI — opportunity landscape, job map, impact simulation, evidence, direct capture, settings — opens beside the conversation, never on top of it. |
45: 
46: Replies render Markdown (headings, lists, emphasis, inline and fenced code).
47: Tool calls appear inline as small trace chips while the agent works.
48: 
49: ## 1. Web — production build (recommended for a quick look)
50: 
51: ```bash
52: npm --prefix apps/studio run build   # build the SPA into apps/studio/dist
53: python scripts/dev.py            # starts MCP :8000 + sidecar :8100
54: ```
55: 
56: | Service | URL |
57: |---|---|
58: | MCP Server | http://localhost:8000/mcp |
59: | Living Studio | http://127.0.0.1:8100 |
60: 
61: `python scripts/dev.py` starts both processes concurrently; press **Ctrl+C** to
62: stop both.
63: 
64: ## 2. Web — dev with hot reload
65: 
66: Vite proxies `/api` to the sidecar:
67: 
68: ```bash
69: npm --prefix apps/studio run dev:full   # MCP + sidecar + Vite together
70: # open http://localhost:5173
71: ```
72: 
73: ## 3. Desktop — Tauri 2
74: 
75: The app spawns the MCP server and sidecar itself:
76: 
77: ```bash
78: npm --prefix apps/studio run tauri dev     # dev window
79: npm --prefix apps/studio run tauri build   # bundles: .deb / .AppImage (Linux), .app / .dmg (macOS), .msi / .exe (Windows)
80: ```
81: 
82: > [!NOTE]
83: > **Tauri prerequisites.** The desktop build needs the WebKitGTK toolchain and
84: > Rust 1.90+. On Debian/Ubuntu:
85: >
86: > ```bash
87: > sudo apt-get install -y libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev build-essential pkg-config curl wget file \
88: >   libxdo-dev libssl-dev libayatana-appindicator3-dev librsvg2-dev patchelf xdg-utils libfuse2t64
89: > ```
90: >
91: > The Tauri CLI ships as the `@tauri-apps/cli` npm dev dependency
92: > (`npm --prefix apps/studio run tauri`). The sidecar is launched with
93: > `uv run python -m …` from the repository root; if the app cannot locate the
94: > repo root, set `AGENTIC_ODI_REPO_ROOT`.
95: 
96: ## Desktop signing & updater secrets
97: 
98: Self-updating and code signing are **env-driven**: if a secret is absent, an
99: unsigned artifact is produced instead of failing. CI reads these from GitHub
100: Actions secrets.
101: 
102: | Secret | Purpose |
103: |---|---|
104: | `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY` | Signs updater artifacts (`.sig`) and the `latest.json` manifest. A tagged release fails loudly without it. Generate with `npm --prefix apps/studio run tauri signer generate`. |
105: | `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD` | Password for the private key (optional when the key has none). |
106: | `APPLE_CERTIFICATE` / `APPLE_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` | macOS Developer ID certificate (base64 `.p12`) and its password. |
107: | `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY` | macOS signing identity. |
108: | `APPLE_ID` / `APPLE_PASSWORD` / `APPLE_TEAM_ID` | macOS notarization credentials. |
109: | `WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE` / `WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` | Windows Authenticode PFX (base64) and its password; imported by CI and injected into the bundle config. |
110: 
111: Releases are published by `.github/workflows/tauri-release.yml` when a `v*` tag
112: is pushed. The desktop app checks for updates on startup and via
113: **Settings → Check for updates**.
114: 
115: ### Managing the updater signing key
116: 
117: The updater key pair authenticates release artifacts so an installed app can
118: verify that an auto-update genuinely came from you. The **public** key is
119: embedded in `apps/studio/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json` (`plugins.updater.pubkey`) and is
120: safe to commit. The **private** key must never be committed, logged, printed in
121: CI, or attached to a build artifact.
122: 
123: 1. **Generate a key pair** (only if you need a new one). Leave `-p ""` for a
124:    passwordless key, or pass a password and remember it:
125: 
126:    ```bash
127:    npm --prefix apps/studio run tauri signer generate -- -w ./living-studio.key -p "" -f
128:    ```
129: 
130:    This writes `living-studio.key` (private, `0600`) and `living-studio.key.pub`
131:    (public).
132: 
133: 2. **Paste the public key** into `apps/studio/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json`:
134: 
135:    ```jsonc
136:    {
137:      "plugins": {
138:        "updater": {
139:          "endpoints": ["https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/releases/latest/download/latest.json"],
140:          "pubkey": "<contents of living-studio.key.pub>"
141:        }
142:      }
143:    }
144:    ```
145: 
146: 3. **Store the private key outside the repository** (the repo root is
147:    git-tracked; a sibling directory is not), with restricted permissions:
148: 
149:    ```bash
150:    mkdir -p ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys && chmod 700 ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys
151:    mv living-studio.key ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/
152:    chmod 600 ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/living-studio.key
153:    ```
154: 
155:    Move it to a long-term secret store (password manager, 1Password/Bitwarden/
156:    Vault, or a private encrypted backup) when you decide where that lives.
157:    Losing it means future releases can no longer be signed for existing
158:    installs.
159: 
160: 4. **Add the private key as a GitHub Actions secret** (Settings → Secrets and
161:    variables → Actions → New repository secret), or via the CLI:
162: 
163:    ```bash
164:    gh secret set TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY < ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/living-studio.key
165:    gh secret set TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD --body ""   # only if you set a password
166:    ```
167: 
168: 5. **Verify** the secrets exist (values are never displayed):
169: 
170:    ```bash
171:    gh secret list
172:    ```
173: 
174: 6. **Rotate** by repeating steps 1–4, then publishing a release signed with the
175:    new key. Existing installs still verify against the public key compiled into
176:    their binary, so keep the old private key usable and publish the new public
177:    key ahead of the cut-over.
178: 
179: > [!CAUTION]
180: > If the private key leaks, treat auto-updates as compromised: generate a new
181: > pair, rotate the Actions secret, and publish a freshly signed release.
182: 
183: > [!IMPORTANT]
184: > **Migration note.** The Streamlit UI has been removed. The Living Studio now
185: > lives in `apps/studio/` (browser SPA + Tauri desktop app) and is served by the
186: > `apps/studio-api` sidecar on port **8100** (previously Streamlit's `8501`).
187: > Start everything with `python scripts/dev.py`. All `AGENTIC_ODI_*` environment
188: > variable names, the demo dataset, and the ODI formulas are unchanged.
189: 
190: ## Connecting an LLM
191: 
192: The Studio needs an OpenAI-compatible LLM backend with tool-calling support to
193: drive the agent. For a fully local setup, see
194: [Local LLM Backend](local-llm.md).
195: 
196: ## Agent-Driven Testing
197: 
198: Type `/dev` in the AI assistant to trigger the full automated workflow: it starts
199: both processes, opens the browser, sends a test message, and reports the results.
200: 
201: Type `/test` to have the agent run all tests and report the results
202: automatically.

> repo root, set `AGENTIC_ODI_REPO_ROOT`.

## Desktop signing & updater secrets

Self-updating and code signing are **env-driven**: if a secret is absent, an
unsigned artifact is produced instead of failing. CI reads these from GitHub
Actions secrets.

| Secret | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY` | Signs updater artifacts (`.sig`) and the `latest.json` manifest. A tagged release fails loudly without it. Generate with `npm --prefix apps/studio run tauri signer generate`. |
| `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD` | Password for the private key (optional when the key has none). |
| `APPLE_CERTIFICATE` / `APPLE_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` | macOS Developer ID certificate (base64 `.p12`) and its password. |
| `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY` | macOS signing identity. |
| `APPLE_ID` / `APPLE_PASSWORD` / `APPLE_TEAM_ID` | macOS notarization credentials. |
| `WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE` / `WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` | Windows Authenticode PFX (base64) and its password; imported by CI and injected into the bundle config. |

Releases are published by `.github/workflows/tauri-release.yml` when a `v*` tag
is pushed. The desktop app checks for updates on startup and via
**Settings → Check for updates**.

### Managing the updater signing key

The updater key pair authenticates release artifacts so an installed app can
verify that an auto-update genuinely came from you. The **public** key is
embedded in `apps/studio/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json` (`plugins.updater.pubkey`) and is
safe to commit. The **private** key must never be committed, logged, printed in
CI, or attached to a build artifact.

1. **Generate a key pair** (only if you need a new one). Leave `-p ""` for a
   passwordless key, or pass a password and remember it:

   ```bash
   npm --prefix apps/studio run tauri signer generate -- -w ./living-studio.key -p "" -f
   ```

   This writes `living-studio.key` (private, `0600`) and `living-studio.key.pub`
   (public).

2. **Paste the public key** into `apps/studio/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json`:

   ```jsonc
   {
     "plugins": {
       "updater": {
         "endpoints": ["https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/releases/latest/download/latest.json"],
         "pubkey": "<contents of living-studio.key.pub>"
       }
     }
   }
   ```

3. **Store the private key outside the repository** (the repo root is
   git-tracked; a sibling directory is not), with restricted permissions:

   ```bash
   mkdir -p ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys && chmod 700 ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys
   mv living-studio.key ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/
   chmod 600 ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/living-studio.key
   ```

   Move it to a long-term secret store (password manager, 1Password/Bitwarden/
   Vault, or a private encrypted backup) when you decide where that lives.
   Losing it means future releases can no longer be signed for existing
   installs.

4. **Add the private key as a GitHub Actions secret** (Settings → Secrets and
   variables → Actions → New repository secret), or via the CLI:

   ```bash
   gh secret set TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY < ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/living-studio.key
   gh secret set TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD --body ""   # only if you set a password
   ```

5. **Verify** the secrets exist (values are never displayed):

   ```bash
   gh secret list
   ```

6. **Rotate** by repeating steps 1–4, then publishing a release signed with the
   new key. Existing installs still verify against the public key compiled into
   their binary, so keep the old private key usable and publish the new public
   key ahead of the cut-over.

> [!CAUTION]
> If the private key leaks, treat auto-updates as compromised: generate a new
> pair, rotate the Actions secret, and publish a freshly signed release.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Migration note.** The Streamlit UI has been removed. The Living Studio now
> lives in `apps/studio/` (browser SPA + Tauri desktop app) and is served by the
> `apps/studio-api` sidecar on port **8100** (previously Streamlit's `8501`).
> Start everything with `python scripts/dev.py`. All `AGENTIC_ODI_*` environment
> variable names, the demo dataset, and the ODI formulas are unchanged.

## Connecting an LLM

The Studio needs an OpenAI-compatible LLM backend with tool-calling support to
drive the agent. For a fully local setup, see
[Local LLM Backend](local-llm.md).

## Agent-Driven Testing

Type `/dev` in the AI assistant to trigger the full automated workflow: it starts
both processes, opens the browser, sends a test message, and reports the results.

Type `/test` to have the agent run all tests and report the results
automatically.
